processing: A sun-dried green tea (shaiqing) made from the old large-leaf arbor trees around Madeng village. As with other sun-dried Yunnan greens, the leaf is fixed, rolled and dried in the sun rather than baked.
harvest_season: Spring tea is the lot people talk about; little is documented about exact picking dates or later flushes.
appearance_dry: Tight, slender strands of a fresh green colour with visible down.
appearance_wet: Plump buds and leaves, tender green and bright.
taste_profile: Fresh and brisk with a full, mellow body and a returning sweetness; the lasting aroma is described as cooked chestnut.

brewing.notes: These are ordinary starting points for a large-leaf Yunnan green, not a local rule. It is known for lasting several steeps, and locally it is also praised cold-steeped, so try a jar in the fridge.

vintage_note: Usually for this class, a Yunnan green is bought from the current year's spring picking and drunk while fresh. Spring lots are the ones named in accounts of Madeng; little is documented about how it is graded or dated on the market today.
description:
Madeng Cha is a green tea from Madeng village in Zhedong, Zhenyuan county, in the Ailao mountain country of Pu'er. It comes from large-leaf arbor trees rather than the small-leaf bushes behind most Chinese greens, and that gives it more body than the colour suggests.

Traditionally it is a sun-dried tea, made from an old tree population of around 500 mu that villagers have long picked. Sun-drying is the same broad approach used for the raw material of pu-erh, but Madeng is treated and drunk as a green tea.

Expect clear yellow-green liquor, a fresh and brisk first impression, then a mellow sweetness that comes back after swallowing. Chestnut is the aroma most often named. It holds up to repeat steeping, and it is also recommended cold-steeped. A local selling point is that it leaves little stain on the cup.

This is a regional name with little international presence, so ask where in Zhenyuan a tea was picked and in what year. Little independent documentation exists to help you check a label.
history:
Local accounts give the tea a history of over 200 years and say it went as tribute before 1949, with very small output. A legend from the Qing period says rebel soldiers under Li Xuedong, an officer of Li Wenxue's uprising, fell ill in the Ailao mountains and recovered by drinking the local tea. It is a story, not a record.

The firmer dates are modern: it is reported as one of Yunnan's eight famous teas at a provincial tea appraisal in 1981, and Thailand's Princess Sirindhorn is said to have praised it at a provincial banquet in May 1990 and been given spring tea to take home. Plantings are reported to have grown to over 1,000 mu after 1949.
